papers.title: Galois scalar extension of simple Lie algebras
papers.label: arXiv:2611.34409v1

summary.background:
- Lie algebra: a vector space with a bracket operation satisfying certain rules, used to describe symmetries (e.g., of continuous transformations).
- Simple Lie algebra: one with no nontrivial proper ideals (no smaller sub-structures closed under the bracket that could be split off).
- Field: a number-like system where addition, subtraction, multiplication and division work (e.g., rationals, real numbers, finite fields with a prime number of elements).
- Field extension: a larger field containing the original, e.g., adding a square root of 2 to the rationals; Galois means it has a rich symmetry group.
- Scalar extension (tensoring with a field): building a new algebra over the bigger field from an algebra over the smaller one.
- Centroid: the set of linear maps that commute with the bracket up to scalar multiplication; its dimension is an invariant.
- Direct sum: placing several copies of an object side by side with no interaction.
summary.one_liner: The paper studies how simple finite-dimensional Lie algebras behave under scalar extension by a finite Galois field extension, giving a splitting criterion for the extended algebra, a simplicity result for prime-order cyclic extensions, and the invariance of the dimension of the centroid, with an application to finite fields.
summary.plain: The paper looks at a family of algebraic structures called simple Lie algebras and asks what happens when you enlarge the number system they are built over, using a Galois extension (a standard way of adding new numbers such as square roots while keeping a symmetry structure). The authors show that under a stated condition the enlarged structure splits into several identical copies of a simpler object, and that in certain prime-order cases with no such copy it stays simple. They also show that a certain invariant, the dimension of the centroid, does not change under these extensions, and use this to work out the centroids over finite fields.
summary.why: The results give a general way to carry classification and structure results from one ground field to another, which is a recurring theme in algebra. The text itself does not discuss applications beyond the centroid computation over finite fields, so the wider reach is uncertain.

papers.abstract: We investigate the behaviour of simple finite-dimensional Lie algebras under finite Galois field extensions. Given a simple Lie algebra $L$ over a field $\mathbb{F}$ and a finite Galois extension $\mathbb{K}/\mathbb{F}$ of degree $n = [\mathbb{K}:\mathbb{F}]$, we prove that if $L$ is isomorphic to a $\mathbb{K}$-Lie algebra $S$ viewed as an $\mathbb{F}$-algebra, then the scalar extension $L \otimes_{\mathbb{F}} \mathbb{K}$ is isomorphic to the direct sum of $n$ copies of $S$. Furthermore, for cyclic extensions of order a prime number, we show that if no such $\mathbb{K}$-Lie algebra $S$ exists, the extended algebra $L \otimes_{\mathbb{F}} \mathbb{K}$ remains simple. This framework provides a general mechanism to transfer structural and classification results across different ground fields. In addition, we examine the centroids of simple Lie algebras, proving that the dimension of the space of centroids is invariant under finite field extensions. As an application, we explicitly determine the structure of the spaces of centroids for simple Lie algebras over finite fields.

papers.title: Normal abelian subgroups of order 5^6 in finite 5-groups
papers.label: arXiv:2611.34205v1

summary.background:
- Group: a set of symmetries (or abstract elements) with a rule for combining them.
- Finite 5-group: a group whose size is a power of 5.
- Abelian subgroup: a sub-collection in which elements commute, so the order of combining them does not matter.
- Normal subgroup: a sub-collection that stays unchanged under conjugation (re-labelling by other group elements).
- Elementary abelian: abelian and every non-identity element has order 5.
- Order 5^6: the sub-collection has 5^6 = 15625 elements.
- Kourovka Notebook: a public list of open problems in group theory.
- Commutator pairing, isotropic subgroup, plane cubic over GF(5): tools from linear and algebraic structure over the field with five elements; the text uses them only in outline.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves that every finite 5-group containing an abelian subgroup of order 5^6 also has a normal abelian subgroup of that order (elementary abelian when the given one is), settling the last open case n=6 of Kourovka Notebook Problem 21.51 for p=5.
summary.plain: The paper studies finite groups built from symmetry-like operations where every element has a power-of-five size. It asks whether a certain kind of "flat, evenly-behaved" sub-collection of a given size that exists inside such a group must also exist in a stable, well-positioned form. The author settles the last open case of this question for sub-collections of size 5 to the sixth power, using a minimal counterexample argument.
summary.why: It closes a listed open problem from a well-known problem collection, and together with earlier results it fixes exactly which sizes the statement holds for. The text does not indicate wider applications beyond group theory.

papers.abstract: A finite 5-group containing an abelian subgroup of order 5^6 has a normal abelian subgroup of that order. If the given subgroup is elementary abelian, the normal subgroup can be chosen elementary abelian. This resolves n=6, the last open case of both parts of Problem~21.51 of the Kourovka Notebook for p=5. Together with earlier results, it follows that 1\le n\le 6 is the exact range in which each assertion holds for every finite 5-group at subgroup order 5^n. In a minimal counterexample, five conjugate abelian subgroups generate a group of class at most three. In class two we construct invariant isotropic subgroups for the commutator pairing. In class three the Jacobi identity produces a nonzero plane cubic over the field of five elements. The five conjugate subgroups give five distinct singular points spanning the plane, which forces the cubic to vanish.

papers.title: Gorenstein symmetry can fail for noetherian rings
papers.label: arXiv:2611.32871v1

summary.background:
- Ring: a set with addition and multiplication, where multiplication need not commute.
- Left and right modules: ways the ring's elements act on other objects from the left or the right; a ring can behave differently on each side.
- Noetherian ring: a ring in which every chain of ideals eventually stops growing, a common finiteness condition.
- Injective dimension: a number measuring how far a module is from being "injective" (a strong extension property); small is nicer, infinite means it never settles.
- Gorenstein symmetry: the expectation that the left and right injective dimensions of a ring agree when both are finite.
- Dualizing complex and Rickard-Keller injective generation: more technical structures in the derived category used to study these modules.
summary.one_liner: The paper constructs a two-sided noetherian ring whose injective dimension is 1 on the left and infinite on the right, showing that Gorenstein symmetry can fail for such rings, and it also studies dualizing complexes and injective generation over a field of characteristic not 2.
summary.plain: This is a pure-mathematics paper about algebraic structures called rings, which are sets of numbers or objects that can be added and multiplied. The question is whether a certain measure of how "well-behaved" a ring is comes out the same whether you look at the ring from the left or from the right. The authors build an example where the two sides give very different answers, so the expected symmetry does not hold.
summary.why: Gorenstein symmetry is a long-standing expected property in ring theory, and the paper shows that it can fail even for rings that are noetherian, a fairly tame and well-studied class. The text does not say what wider applications it has, so its importance beyond this area is unclear.

papers.abstract: We construct a two-sided noetherian ring $A$ which has injective dimension $1$ as a left module over itself and infinite injective dimension as a right module over itself. This shows that Gorenstein symmetry can fail for two-sided noetherian rings. It is further shown that there is such an example over any field of characteristic different than $2$, that it has a dualizing complex, and that its derived category of right modules does not satisfy injective-generation in the sense of Rickard-Keller.

papers.title: The optimal exponent in the Babai-Goodman-Pyber theorem
papers.label: arXiv:2611.32149v1

summary.background:
- Finite group: a set of symmetries (or permutations) with finitely many elements, combined by composition.
- Subgroup: a smaller group sitting inside a larger one; [X:H] is the index, roughly how many copies of H fill X.
- Soluble (solvable) group: one that can be built from abelian (commutative) pieces in successive layers; it is the "simple-ish" end of group structure.
- Normal subgroup: one that is preserved under conjugation (relabeling by group elements); the radical Rad(X) is the largest soluble normal subgroup.
- Finite simple group: a finite group with no nontrivial normal subgroups; these are the building blocks of all finite groups.
- Automorphism group: the group of structure-preserving relabelings of a group.
- Exponent and coefficient: c is the power to which the index is raised; 24^{-1/3} is a multiplicative constant.
- PSL_2(8): a specific finite simple group used as the extremal example.
summary.one_liner: The paper determines the optimal exponent c in the Babai-Goodman-Pyber bound [X:Rad(X)] ≤ [X:H]^c for finite groups, showing the least possible c is 1+log_9(168·24^{1/3}) ≈ 3.8141, with a sharper coefficient 24^{-1/3} for nonsoluble groups, and reduces the question to soluble subgroups of automorphism groups of finite simple groups.
summary.plain: This is about finite groups, which are collections of symmetries that can be combined, and how large their non-solvable core is compared with a solvable subgroup (a subgroup whose structure is built up in simple layered steps). The paper gives the smallest exponent for which a known size-comparison inequality holds, and it shows the answer is about 3.81. For groups that are not solvable, it also gives a tighter version of the inequality with a specific constant, and it uses examples based on the group PSL_2(8) to show these values cannot be improved.
summary.why: It settles the exact best constant in a known theorem of Babai, Goodman and Pyber, so the question of how sharp that theorem is now has a definite answer. The text does not say what wider applications it has, so any connection beyond group theory is unclear from the text alone.

papers.abstract: Babai, Goodman and Pyber proved that there exists an absolute constant $c$ such that $[X:\operatorname{Rad}(X)]\le [X:H]^c$ for every finite group $X$ and every soluble subgroup $H\le X$, where $\operatorname{Rad}(X)$ denotes the largest soluble normal subgroup of $X$. We prove that the least possible value of $c$ is $b_0=1+\log_9(168\cdot 24^{1/3})\approx3.8141$. For nonsoluble $X$, we obtain the stronger inequality $[X:\operatorname{Rad}(X)]\le 24^{-1/3}[X:H]^{b_0}$, and the coefficient $24^{-1/3}$ is optimal for this exponent. We reduce the problem to bounds on soluble subgroups of automorphism groups of finite simple groups. Examples based on $\operatorname{PSL}_2(8)$ establish sharpness.

papers.title: The Fourth-Power Formula for the Antipode in AS-Gorenstein Hopf Algebras
papers.label: arXiv:2611.30340v1

summary.background:
- Hopf algebra: an algebraic structure combining multiplication, comultiplication and an antipode (a kind of inverse-like map), used to describe symmetries.
- Antipode S: a linear map generalizing inversion; its fourth power S^4 is the object of the formula.
- Radford's S^4 formula: a known result for finite-dimensional Hopf algebras expressing S^4 as conjugation by a group-like element.
- AS-Gorenstein property: a homological regularity condition (from Artin–Schelter) that allows homological integrals to be defined.
- Homological integrals and Yetter–Drinfeld modules: advanced tools from homological algebra and representation theory used to carry out the argument.
- Coradical, noetherian, faithfully flat: standard technical conditions under which the main results hold.
summary.one_liner:
The paper proves an S^4 formula for the antipode of left AS-Gorenstein Hopf algebras (infinite-dimensional generalization of Radford's finite-dimensional result), via a twisted Yetter–Drinfeld structure on the space of left homological integrals, and applies it to antipode bijectivity and finite-order bounds.</one_liner>
<parameter name="plain">The paper studies a class of algebraic structures called Hopf algebras, which carry a built-in "reversal" map called the antipode. It shows that applying this reversal four times returns to the start up to a controlled twist, extending a known result that was previously proved only for finite-dimensional cases. The authors also use this formula to say when the reversal map is a bijection and to give explicit bounds on how many repetitions are needed in certain settings.
summary.why: The result extends a known formula (Radford's S^4 formula) to a much broader, infinite-dimensional class, and refines an earlier formula by Brown and Zhang by identifying a specific conjugating element. The text does not indicate wider applications beyond algebra, so its significance is mainly within this area of research.

papers.abstract: AS-Gorenstein Hopf algebras, for which homological integrals are defined, form a broad class of (infinite-dimensional) Hopf algebras. We establish an $S^4$ formula for left AS-Gorenstein Hopf algebras, thereby generalizing Radford's $S^4$ formula for finite-dimensional Hopf algebras and refining the formula of Brown and Zhang by identifying a group-like conjugating element in the Hopf algebra $H$. Our approach is to endow the space of left homological integrals $\int^{\ell}_H$ with a canonical right $H^*$-module structure compatible with its natural right $H$-action. If the $H^*$-action is rational, then $\int^{\ell}_H$ carries a canonical $(\mathrm{id}_H,S^4)$-twisted right-left Yetter--Drinfeld module structure. The right $H$-action and left $H$-coaction on this one-dimensional space determine a character and a group-like element in $H$, respectively; the twisted Yetter--Drinfeld compatibility condition then yields the $S^4$ formula. The $H^*$-action on $\int^{\ell}_H$ is rational if either the coradical of $H$ is coreflexive or the trivial left module $\Bbbk$ admits a finitely generated projective resolution. In particular, the latter condition holds when $H$ is left noetherian. We also establish a corresponding result for right AS-co-Gorenstein Hopf algebras with coreflexive coradical. As applications, we use the $S^4$ formula to study the bijectivity of the antipode and derive explicit finite-order bounds when $H$ is module-finite and faithfully flat over a central right coideal subalgebra, or finitely cogenerated and faithfully coflat over a cocentral quotient.

papers.title: Products of supersoluble groups
papers.label: arXiv:2611.29591v1

summary.background:
- Finite group: a group with finitely many elements, such as the symmetries of a shape.
- Product of subgroups G = AB: every element of G can be written as a times b, with a in A and b in B.
- Supersoluble group: a group whose structure breaks into a chain of cyclic pieces, a fairly restricted kind of solvable group.
- Soluble (solvable) group: a group that can be built step by step from abelian (commutative) pieces.
- Composition factor: the simple building blocks that a finite group is assembled from.
- PSL_2(p): a specific simple non-abelian group, defined for each prime p.
- Nonsoluble length: how many layers of non-solvable structure the group has, counted in stages.
summary.one_liner: If a finite group is a product of two supersoluble subgroups, then its nonabelian composition factors are all PSL_2(p) with p at least 5, and its nonsoluble length is at most one.
summary.plain: This paper is about finite groups, which are collections of symmetries that can be combined, and how they can be built from smaller pieces. It asks what happens when a group can be written as the product of two "supersoluble" subgroups, which are groups that are especially simple in structure. The author shows that any non-abelian building blocks of such a group must be one specific family of groups, and that the group is only mildly complicated in how it stacks non-solvable layers.
summary.why: This is a structural classification result within group theory: it narrows down exactly what the pieces of a factorised group can look like. The text does not say what wider applications it has, so any connection beyond pure algebra is unclear from the summary alone.

papers.abstract: Let $G=AB$ be a finite group, where $A$ and $B$ are supersoluble. We prove that every nonabelian composition factor of $G$ is isomorphic to $\PSL_2(p)$ for some prime $p\ge5$ and that the nonsoluble length of $G$ is at most one.

papers.title: On coherence of enveloping algebras of infinite-dimensional Lie algebras
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27824v1

summary.background:
- Lie algebra: a vector space with a bracket operation, used to describe continuous symmetries.
- Universal enveloping algebra U(g): a ring built from a Lie algebra g that encodes its representations.
- Loop algebra: functions from a circle (or Laurent polynomials) with values in a finite-dimensional Lie algebra.
- Witt algebra: the derivations of Laurent polynomials, an infinite-dimensional example.
- Coherent ring: a ring where finitely generated one-sided ideals are finitely presented; a finiteness property.
- Noetherian ring: every ideal is finitely generated; coherence is a weaker related condition.
- Nilpotent: a Lie algebra whose repeated brackets eventually vanish.
- Graded and filtered rings: rings split into pieces indexed by integers or ordered by a size-like filtration; the Rees ring links the two.
summary.one_liner: The paper determines when universal enveloping algebras of infinite-dimensional Lie algebras (notably loop algebras and the Witt algebra) are coherent, and studies coherence of related graded and filtered rings.
summary.plain: The paper studies a property called "coherence" for a family of algebraic structures built from infinite-dimensional symmetry-like objects (Lie algebras). Coherence is a tidy-behaviour condition: roughly, certain systems of equations have solutions that are finitely described. The authors show that for loop algebras the property holds exactly when the underlying finite-dimensional algebra is nilpotent, and they find that several specific examples fail it.
summary.why: It sharpens what is known about which infinite-dimensional algebras behave well under standard finiteness conditions, and it extends earlier work on non-Noetherianity of the Witt-algebra enveloping algebra. The text does not indicate further applications beyond this algebraic classification.

papers.abstract: We investigate when the universal enveloping algebra $U(\mathfrak{g})$ of an infinite-dimensional Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ is coherent. We show that if $\mathfrak{g}$ is the loop algebra of a finite-dimensional Lie algebra $\mathfrak{h}$ then $U(\mathfrak{g})$ is coherent exactly when $\mathfrak{h}$ is nilpotent. As a consequence, we show that $U(\mathfrak{g})$ is not coherent if $\mathfrak{g}$ is complex, simple, $\mathbb{Z}$-graded, of polynomially bounded growth, and not isomorphic to the Witt algebra $W = \mathrm{Der} \mathbb{C}[t,t^{-1}]$ or its one-sided version. We also demonstrate that the homomorphic image of $U(W)$ used to prove non-Noetherianity of $U(W)$ in previous work of the first author and Walton is not coherent. On the other hand, we establish that two closely related connected graded rings are graded coherent. Finally, we prove that any exhaustively filtered ring is coherent if its Rees ring is graded coherent.

papers.title: Large orbits of $p$-groups on conjugacy classes of arbitrary finite groups
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27916v1

summary.background:
- Finite group: a group with finitely many elements, such as the symmetries of a finite object.
- p-group: a group whose size is a power of a prime p.
- Acting coprimely and faithfully: P applies symmetries to H in a way that is nontrivial and does not share prime factors with H's order in a problematic way.
- Conjugacy class: a set of elements of H that are equivalent under relabeling by H itself.
- Stabilizer / orbit: the stabilizer is the set of symmetries in P fixing a given class; the orbit is the set of classes it moves it to. Large orbit means small stabilizer.
- Solvable group: a group built up by stacking simple pieces that are abelian; nonsolvable groups contain more complex simple pieces.
- Classification of finite simple groups: a large completed classification of the basic building blocks of finite groups, used as a tool here.
- Irreducible character and inertia group: basic objects of representation theory; the inertia group is the set of symmetries that preserve a given character.
summary.one_liner: The paper extends a known result on large orbits of coprime p-group actions from solvable to arbitrary finite groups, showing via the classification of finite simple groups that some conjugacy class (or irreducible character) has stabilizer of order at most |P|^{1/2}, with a new nonsolvable family attaining the bound.
summary.plain: This paper is about symmetries of finite groups: a small group P of symmetries (of prime-power size) acts on a finite group H, and the question is how many elements of H P can leave mostly in place. The author-level result is that, for every such action, some conjugacy class of H has a stabilizer in P of size at most the square root of |P|. A previous paper had proved this only when H is solvable, and this paper removes that restriction, using the classification of finite simple groups.
summary.why: The bound is sharp: the text says it is attained, and the paper gives a new family of nonsolvable examples where it is reached. The result also gives, as a consequence, an irreducible character of H whose inertia group in P is small, which links the question to representation theory; the text does not say more about wider applications.

papers.abstract: Let $P$ be a $p$-group that acts faithfully and coprimely on a finite group $H$. In a previous paper it was shown that if $H$ is solvable, then there exists a conjugacy class $c$ of $H$ whose stabilizer in $P$ has order at most $|P|^{1/2}$, and that this bound is best possible. In this paper we remove the hypothesis that $H$ is solvable. As a consequence, there always exists an irreducible character of $H$ whose inertia group in $P$ has order at most $|P|^{1/2}$. The proof depends on the classification of finite simple groups. Its main new ingredient is a result on quasiprimitive linear actions of $p$-nilpotent groups which shows that the elements acting as field automorphisms can be ignored when one looks for vectors with small stabilizers. We also present a new family of examples, with nonsolvable $H$, in which the bound is attained.
